result.sentence: This home's 14,400 kWh a year is 20% more than the utility's average home and 20% more than the state's (EIA-861, 2025).

work.method: Sum the latest 12 periods, or scale fewer to 365 days by the days they cover. Compare with EIA-861's average residential use per customer (residential sales ÷ residential customers) for the utility and the state, as a percent difference. Then compare the highest and lowest periods by kWh per day.
steps: A year of use: 14,400 kWh, the sum of the latest 12 periods (365 days).
The utility's average home: 12,000 kWh a year (residential sales ÷ residential customers, EIA-861, 2025). 14,400 kWh ÷ 12,000 kWh − 1 = 20%.
The state's average home: 12,000 kWh a year (EIA-861, 2025). 14,400 kWh ÷ 12,000 kWh − 1 = 20%.
These are averages across homes of every size and heating type. EIA-861 publishes no distribution, so there is no percentile or rank.
Highest period: February 1, 2025 to February 28, 2025, 42.9 kWh a day. Lowest: January 1, 2025 to January 31, 2025, 38.7 kWh a day. The highest is 1.1× the lowest.
assumptions: State averages leave out delivery-only rows, whose customers EIA also counts under the company that sells them energy; this is how EIA's Table 5A counts them.
A partial year is scaled by days, so a year with a hot summer and a mild winter in the missing months reads high or low.

result.sentence: From 213 days, we estimate 13,651 kWh a year. That is 13.8% more than the utility's average home and 13.8% more than the state's (EIA-861, 2025).

work.method: Sum the latest 12 periods, or scale fewer to 365 days by the days they cover. Compare with EIA-861's average residential use per customer (residential sales ÷ residential customers) for the utility and the state, as a percent difference. Then compare the highest and lowest periods by kWh per day.
steps: A year of use: 13,651 kWh, estimated from 213 days: 7,966 kWh × 365 ÷ 213.
The utility's average home: 12,000 kWh a year (residential sales ÷ residential customers, EIA-861, 2025). 13,651 kWh ÷ 12,000 kWh − 1 = 13.8%.
The state's average home: 12,000 kWh a year (EIA-861, 2025). 13,651 kWh ÷ 12,000 kWh − 1 = 13.8%.
These are averages across homes of every size and heating type. EIA-861 publishes no distribution, so there is no percentile or rank.
Highest period: January 1, 2026 to January 31, 2026, 62 kWh a day. Lowest: May 1, 2026 to May 31, 2026, 24 kWh a day. The highest is 2.6× the lowest.
A swing above 1.5× often has a cause worth checking: electric heating, air conditioning, a pool or spa pump, electric vehicle charging. These are things to check, not a diagnosis.

A partial year is scaled by days, so a year with a hot summer and a mild winter in the missing months reads high or low.
